name: Fatima Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Fatima. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on nights at Kerrow Plastics, an injection moulding plant that makes clips and door trims for car makers. I clock in at ten, take over press 7 from the day girl, and for eight hours I pull parts off, trim the flash, which is the thin bit of extra plastic, and pack them into crates. Press 7 is the oldest one, 450 tonnes, and it sulks when it's cold.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's honest work, you can count what you made. I like the union, honestly, Denise our shop steward has saved my job once already. What wears me out is the short-time weeks. Four times this year they sent us home on 60% pay because a car maker cut its order, and I've got maybe two weeks of money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it out. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. Every year someone says robots are coming to the plastics plant, and every year it's still me pulling clips off press 7 by hand. At the union meeting I'd be the one laughing at the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI was never my worry. Short-time weeks on 60% pay, with two weeks of money in the bank, are my worry. So nothing changes for me, and that's not the same as fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and take every Saturday overtime shift going. I'd stop the Friday takeaway, that's about 30 a week, and try to get one full month saved by summer. And I'd keep paying my union dues, because that's the only insurance I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired more than scared. It's the same worry on a loop, just without a robot in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first if there's another short-time month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone, then the gas if it's summer. Tomás, my partner, and I split the rent down the middle, and rent never goes late, I learned that at 22. Last time I borrowed 200 from my sister and I hated asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything at the plant changing anyway, even in this quiet picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They put a camera on press 3 last year that checks parts for flash. It saves Priya on that press maybe five minutes an hour, nothing more. If that's all AI ever is, fine by me.

say: I'd tell the union branch the **robot hype** was wrong again.
I'd point out it's still **people pulling clips** off the presses by hand.
think: My real worry is **short-time weeks** on 60% pay, not AI.
With about **two weeks saved**, one bad car order hurts every time.
do: Take every **Saturday overtime** shift on press 7.
Stop the Friday takeaway and save **about 30 a week** towards one month's cushion.
Keep paying **union dues** as the only insurance she has.
feel: **Tired** more than scared, the same worry on a loop.
S0.quote: AI was never my worry. Short-time weeks on 60% pay, with two weeks of money in the bank, are my worry.
fieldNote: Her stress comes from **car-maker orders**, not technology, and it doesn't go away when AI stalls.
She trusts the **shop steward** more than management or any app.
Borrowing 200 from her sister still **stings**; she hates asking for help.

steps.text: Work every Saturday overtime shift going on press 7
Drop the Friday takeaway to save about 30 a week
Keep paying union dues and go to the monthly branch meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what the union says: if robots come in, workers get a say, and the savings don't all go to the owners. I'd share the union's posts online. I'm not going to pretend I have clever opinions about software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The writing and coding stuff doesn't touch me, I don't do any of that. What scares me is the pick-and-place arms, the robot arms that lift parts out of the mould. Slowly, to a manager, means one press a year. My press is the oldest one in the plastics plant, so it's either last in line or scrapped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push Denise to get a written deal: nobody laid off when an arm goes in, they move us to packing or quality instead. I'd say yes to the quality-checking course I skipped last spring, but only if it's in paid hours. And I'd keep putting the takeaway money aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like something's being decided over my head. A bit angry, and a bit small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gloria on the trim bench. She's 58 and her English isn't strong, so if they shuffle people around, she gets left out first. I'd sit with her at the meetings and make sure someone explains things to her properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does any thinking work in your own day change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rota, maybe, that comes from the office. If a computer does the rota, fine, as long as it doesn't start giving me split shifts. Last thing I want is an app telling me when to sleep.

say: I'd repeat the union line that **workers get a say** when robots arrive.
I'd share union posts online but **stay out** of software arguments.
think: The office tasks don't touch her; the **robot arms** on the presses do.
Her old press is either **last in line** or scrapped, and she can't tell which.
do: Push the shop steward for a **written no-layoff deal** when arms go in.
Take the **quality-checking course** she skipped, but only in paid hours.
Keep **saving the takeaway** money every week.
feel: **Angry** and a bit small, like decisions are made over her head.
S1.quote: Slowly, to a manager, means one press a year. My press is the oldest one in the plastics plant, so it's either last in line or scrapped.
fieldNote: She reads "slowly" through a manager's eyes: **one press a year**.
Her loyalty goes to **older colleagues** like Gloria who'd be left out first.
She'll train, but only when the **union negotiates** it into paid hours.

steps.text: Push the shop steward for a written no-layoff deal on robot arms
Sign up for the plant's quality-checking course if it runs in paid hours
Keep putting the 30-a-week takeaway money into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need laws, and fast. Tax the companies that use robots and pay people while they find something else. I'd go to protests, and I've never been to one in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, 2028 itself doesn't scare me as much as 2031. The office people get hit first, the planners and the resin buyers. Then three years later the robot that does my job turns up, and I'll be 32 with nothing but moulding machines on my CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd tell the union we need a plan before 2031, not after. Tomás and I would stop talking about a bigger flat and stay where we are. And I'd have a proper talk with my mum about the back room, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like waiting for a letter you already know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years to AGI and three more for robots, what does that time actually give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In three years I might have one month in the bank instead of half a month. Three years sounds long until you think how little I save. That's not a plan, that's a slightly longer fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomás the night the robots arrive at Kerrow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say his delivery van is probably going too, so we're in it together. We'd probably laugh, because what else do you do. Then in the morning I'd ring my mum and ask about the back room for real.

say: I'd demand **laws now**: a robot tax and pay while people look for work.
I'd go to **protests** for the first time in her life.
think: The office goes first; her **press job** goes about three years later.
At 32 she'd have **only moulding** on her CV.
do: Ask the union for a **plan before 2031**, not after.
Drop the **bigger flat** and stay put with Tomás.
Talk to her mum now about the **back room** as a fallback.
feel: **Sick**, like waiting for a letter she knows is coming.
S2.quote: Three years sounds long until you think how little I save. That's not a plan, that's a slightly longer fall.
fieldNote: The three-year robot gap means little to her because her **savings barely grow**.
Both incomes in the household are **hands-on** and exposed, the van and the press.
She turns to **law and protest** rather than personal retraining.

steps.text: Ask the union branch for a written plan before robots arrive in 2031
Join protests for a robot tax and paid time to find work
Drop the bigger-flat plan and renew the current lease
Agree with her mum on using the back room if wages stop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, but louder, because nobody can say they didn't see it coming. Five years is plenty of time to write laws. If the government doesn't, that's a choice they made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots by 2034 means I'm 35. That's better and worse. Better because I get seven more years of wages, worse because I'd be tempted to do nothing for six of them, and I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd vote for whoever promises a jobs guarantee, and nag everyone on nights to vote too. I'd ask Ray, who leads maintenance, if I can shadow him on Fridays, because someone has to fix the robots for a while. And I'd open a savings account I don't touch and put 50 a month in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, but not sick like the fast one. More like a bag I carry around all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In 2031, before the robots, the thinking AI arrives. What changes at Kerrow that year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office, mostly: planning, ordering resin, the rota. Maybe two or three people upstairs go. On the floor we'd get more short-notice shift switches, but nobody on press 7 loses a job that year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be tempted to do nothing. What would stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Having it in writing. If the union gets a date from the company, like presses get robots in 2034, then I'd move. A vague maybe never makes me move. I've ignored vague maybes my whole life.

say: I'd say five years is **enough time** for laws, so doing nothing is a choice.
I'd tell the night shift to **vote** on it.
think: Robots by 2034 give her **seven more years** of wages.
She admits she'd be **tempted to coast** for most of that time.
do: Vote for a **jobs guarantee** and push colleagues to vote.
Ask the maintenance lead to let her **shadow repairs** on Fridays.
Put **50 a month** into an untouched savings account.
feel: **Heavy** rather than sick, like a bag she carries all day.
S3.quote: A vague maybe never makes me move. I've ignored vague maybes my whole life.
fieldNote: She knows her own **habit of waiting** and names it honestly.
A **written date** from the company would move her more than any warning.
She sees 2031 as an **office year** and 2034 as her year.

steps.text: Vote for the party promising a jobs guarantee
Ask the maintenance lead to let her shadow repairs on Fridays
Put 50 a month into a separate savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so don't waste it. Use it for proper retraining, paid and in work hours, not evening classes for people who are already worn out from nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots in 2039 is half my working life away, I'd be 40. Honestly, I'd keep doing what I do and hope the union sorts it. That's the truth, even if it doesn't sound good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working nights and keep paying dues. Push the union to make paid retraining part of the next pay deal. Anything bigger, I'd leave a few years and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. But I know calm is how I end up doing nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change for you and Tomás?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe kids. We've said in a few years since I was 24. With ten years, we'd still maybe do it, but I'd want the plant to still be open while the baby is small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2036, robots in 2039. Does that order matter for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, my job is all hands. I can barely work the touchscreen on the new press as it is. The office will feel 2036, and I'll feel 2039.

say: I'd call ten years a **gift** that shouldn't be wasted.
I'd want retraining **paid** and in **work hours**, not tired evening classes.
think: She'd be **40** when robots arrive, half her working life away.
Honestly she'd **keep going** and hope the union sorts it.
do: Keep working **nights on press 7** and paying union dues.
Push the union to put **paid retraining** in the next pay deal.
Leave any **bigger decision** for a few years.
feel: **Calmer**, but aware that calm lets her drift.
S4.quote: I know calm is how I end up doing nothing.
fieldNote: Extra time **lowers her fear** but doesn't change her plans.
Her day-to-day worries, the **short-time weeks**, stay the same.
The decade reopens the question of **having children**.

steps.text: Keep working nights on press 7 and paying union dues
Push the union to add paid retraining to the next pay deal
Wait a few years before choosing any new trade

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. The office goes first and the floor gets three years, and three years on my savings is nothing. If a robot takes my press, the company should pay me to retrain for a year, at full wage, not 60%.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask if I'd let a robot train me. I wouldn't, and I know that's stubborn. I learned press 7 from a woman called Ines who'd done it 30 years, and I want the next person to learn from a person too.

headlineQuote: If a robot takes my press, the company should pay me to retrain for a year, at full wage, not 60%.
portrait: Fatima, 27, works **nights** on an **old press** at a car-parts plastics plant.
She has about **two weeks saved** and already loses pay to short-time weeks.
She trusts the **union** and her shop steward far more than managers or technology.
Across the pictures she pushes for **laws and union deals** rather than retraining herself.
She admits she **drifts** when change feels far away, and needs a written date to act.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because three years before robots is nothing on her savings.
whatWouldHelp: A rule that firms pay a **year of retraining** at full wage when a robot takes a job.
